unit_label: BFM Module C unit 7 (courseware unit 25): treasury and asset-liability management

facts.statement: Meaning of ALM (courseware): modern banking is maturity intermediation or risk intermediation: the bank collects deposits of varying maturities and lends for varying maturities, modifying and extending maturities that depositors could not afford, and absorbing market and credit risk. Credit risk is managed through credit supervision; market risk shows as liquidity risk and interest rate risk. Illustration: a 3-year deposit at 8 per cent used for a 90-day bill discounting facility repriced every 90 days; if rates fall to 7 per cent the bank earns a negative spread because the deposit rate is fixed while the lending rate floats; or deposits of average one-year maturity funding long fixed-rate mortgage loans creates a liquidity problem when deposits mature and a negative spread if rates rise. Risks arise from mismatch of assets and liabilities; ALM is protection of the net worth of the bank, managing balance sheet risks that can otherwise cause negative spreads and erosion of net worth.

Liquidity risk and the gap (courseware): liquidity and interest rate are two sides of the same coin; banks are extra sensitive to liquidity risk since they cannot default or delay on obligations; even suspicion of pressure can cause a run on the bank. Liquidity is a positive cash flow: surplus cash, committed credit lines from other banks, liquefiable securities and nostro balances. In ALM, assets are cash inflows on maturity and liabilities cash outflows. The mismatch in each time bucket is the liquidity gap: when sources exceed uses it is a positive gap, when deposits and other outflows exceed inflows it is a negative gap. The central bank prescribes time bands (next day, 2-7 days, 8-14 days, 15-30 days and so on) and limits on the net cumulative negative mismatch in the near buckets as a percentage of cumulative outflows (percentages not taught). Securities classified as liquid must be marketable, since a securities market that dries up makes them illiquid. Contingency measures in the liquidity management policy include standby credit lines from other banks, liquid investments, holding excess securities and borrowing under the liquidity adjustment facility or tri-party repo.

Interest rate risk and repricing gap (courseware): interest rate risk is the risk of erosion of net interest income (NII = interest earned less interest paid) from market rate movements. Example: deposits of Rs 100 crore at 5 per cent with 6-month maturity invested at a fixed 7 per cent for 5 years: when deposits are renewed at 6 per cent the NII falls (2 per cent becomes 1 per cent) and if renewed at 8 per cent it turns negative; in the reverse case (long fixed deposit funding short floating advances) falling rates hurt. Repricing risk is the mismatch between assets and liabilities repricing in a time bucket: assets and liabilities are placed in time buckets by repricing date (not maturity); a fixed-rate bond maturing in 7 years is not repriced until then, a loan that is repriced in 6 months appears in the 6-month-1 year bucket. The gap is rate sensitive assets less rate sensitive liabilities in each bucket, expressed in absolute terms, as a sensitivity ratio (rate sensitive assets to rate sensitive liabilities) or as a percentage; the mismatch is monitored against pre-set limits and can be reduced by swapping fixed to floating or floating to fixed. The central bank requires capital for market risk, including interest rate mismatch and derivatives; other ALM tools include VaR, present value, duration and simulations.

Role of treasury in ALM (courseware): the balance sheet carries large market risk besides credit risk; treasury links core banking with financial markets, so market risk is identified and monitored through treasury. Mismatches cannot be removed by moving assets or liabilities across time bands, and a bank earns profit from some mismatch; treasury uses derivatives and new products to bridge liquidity and interest rate sensitivity gaps. Treasury trading positions create their own market risk, sometimes compensating; treasury hedges only the residual risk. Credit products are increasingly replaced by treasury products (commercial paper in place of working capital, marketable and liquid); treasury monitors exchange and interest rate movements. In many banks the ALM desk is part of the dealing room or an ALCO support group is part of treasury; the Treasury head is a member of the Asset-Liability Committee (ALCO) and contributes to product pricing and policy.

Derivatives in ALM (courseware): derivatives replicate market movements and counter inherent risks of regular products; they need little capital (margin only on exchange traded). They can hedge individual high-value transactions or aggregate balance sheet risk (the latter needs dynamic management). Example 1: a 3-year loan funded by 3-month deposits (cheaper, but liquidity risk and an interest rate risk because the deposit is repriced 12 times); the bank swaps the floating 3-month cost into fixed for 3 years (receives floating T-bill-linked, pays fixed), so the cost of deposits is fixed and the spread on the fixed-rate loan is protected. Example 2: deposit priced at 91-day T-bill plus 1 per cent and the loan yielding T-bill plus 3 per cent (a 2 per cent spread) protected by a swap. Example 3: USD funds borrowed at 3 per cent for 6 months and lent in rupees at 6.5 per cent; forward premium (cost of hedge) 1.5 per cent: spread 6.5 - 3 - 1.5 = 2 per cent. Currency mismatches can be hedged with call options to repay foreign currency loans or put options to protect foreign currency receivables. Treasury helps structure new products: floating deposits and loans linked to a benchmark, index linked securities, bonds with call and put options (embedded options). Limitations: product rates may not follow the benchmark, embedded options such as prepayment cannot be hedged fully, basis risk remains as residual risk, the derivative market must be developed and dealers need skills.

Credit risk and credit derivatives (courseware): treasury credit risk is limited to counterparty dealings within exposure limits, but treasury intertwines with lending through credit substitutes (commercial paper and corporate bonds, where the bond can be marked to market and sold at a discount if credit quality falls, giving more flexibility than a loan) and through securitisation (converting loan receivables into tradable pass-through certificates (PTCs) issued through a special purpose vehicle (SPV), freeing capital for fresh lending; banks with surplus funds may also invest in PTCs). Credit derivatives (credit default swap or credit linked note) separate credit risk from the asset and transfer it to a protection seller for a fee: the protection buyer (the owner of the asset) pays a premium (the credit default spread, an annual percentage of notional) and the protection seller pays principal if the reference entity defaults (credit event). They allow diversification and efficient use of capital but the market is not very liquid. The 2008-09 crisis showed negative aspects: institutions securitised assets without proper assessment and transferred risk to protection sellers whose own credit quality deteriorated (counterparty risk), and credit derivatives are highly leveraged (the fee is a tiny part of notional; if default occurs losses are large). The central bank was cautious but introduced single name credit default swaps on corporate bonds; banks can be market makers and users to hedge banking or trading book exposure; eligibility norms exist (not taught).

Transfer pricing (courseware): transfer pricing fixes the cost of resources and the return on assets of the bank in a rational manner: the treasury notionally buys and sells the deposits and loans of the bank, and the price forms the basis for assessing the profitability of banking activity. Treasury determines the price on the basis of market rates of interest, cost of hedging market risk and cost of maintaining reserve assets. Example: the banking department procures a deposit at 7 per cent but the treasury buys it at its market cost adjusted for hedging and liquidity, say 6 per cent; the difference is borne by the banking department; if the banking department lends at 10 per cent and sells the loan to treasury at the transfer price of 7 per cent, the 3 per cent balance is the risk premium earned by the banking side. Prices vary by tenor and maturity. Once implemented, treasury takes care of liquidity and interest rate risks of the entire bank, and the profits of credit departments reflect only credit risk, net of mismatches. It is useful for assessing branch profitability in a multi-branch environment.

Policy environment (courseware): ALM is effective only with a strong policy foundation; the integrated risk management policy has components: ALM policy (composition of the Asset Liability Management Committee (ALCO), risk measures, monitoring, product pricing, MIS, how to maintain net interest margin); liquidity policy (minimum liquidity, funding of reserve assets, limits on money market exposure, contingent funding and committed credit lines); derivatives policy (norms for use, capital allocation, restrictions, valuation, exposure limits); investment policy (permissible investments, rating and listing norms, SLR and non-SLR investments, private placements, classification and valuation, repos, accounting); composite risk policy for foreign exchange and treasury (merchant and trading positions, securities trading, exposure limits, intra-day and overnight limits, stop-loss, valuation); and transfer pricing policy (methodology, spreads retained by treasury, allocation of costs to branches). They are supplemented by the money laundering prevention policy and a hedging policy for customer risks; credit and operational risk policies are outside ALCO. Requirements: approved at the highest level (Board or a Board committee), compliant with regulations and market codes (FIMMDA, FEDAI), monitored by a committee of senior executives, subject to annual review, and copies filed with the central bank in most cases.

payload.title: Meaning of asset-liability management
payload.core_explanation_md:
Modern banking is **maturity intermediation (risk intermediation)**: the bank takes **deposits of varying maturities** and lends for **different maturities**, absorbing **credit and market risk** that depositors cannot.

**Market risk** appears as **liquidity risk** and **interest rate risk**.

**Examples:** a **3-year fixed deposit at 8 per cent** funding a **90-day bill discounting facility** repriced every 90 days: if rates fall, the **lending rate falls but the deposit rate stays**: **negative spread**. Or **one-year deposits funding long fixed-rate mortgages**: **liquidity problem** at maturity and a **negative spread if rates rise**.

**ALM** manages these **balance sheet mismatches** to **protect the net worth** of the bank.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: ALM is about the gap between when assets and liabilities mature or reprice.

self_check.prompt_text: What does ALM aim to protect?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The net worth of the bank, by managing mismatches between assets and liabilities.

payload.title: Liquidity risk and the liquidity gap
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Liquidity and interest rate are two sides of one coin.** A bank cannot default or delay, and even **suspicion** can cause a **run on the bank**.

**Sources of liquidity:** **surplus cash**, **committed credit lines**, **liquefiable securities**, **nostro balances**.

**In ALM:** assets = **cash inflows** at maturity; liabilities = **cash outflows**. In each **time bucket**:

- **Positive gap** = inflows (sources) exceed outflows (uses).
- **Negative gap** = outflows exceed inflows.

The central bank sets **time bands** (next day, 2-7 days, 8-14 days, 15-30 days...) and **limits on net cumulative negative mismatch** in the near buckets (percentages not taught). **Liquid** securities must truly be **marketable**.

**Contingency measures:** **standby credit lines**, **liquid investments**, **excess securities**, borrowing under the **LAF** or **TREPS**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The risk is not lack of profit but lack of cash at the moment it is needed.

self_check.prompt_text: What is a negative liquidity gap?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A time bucket in which cash outflows exceed cash inflows.

payload.title: Interest rate risk and the repricing gap
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Interest rate risk** = risk of **erosion of net interest income (NII = interest earned - interest paid)**.

Example: **Rs 100 crore of 6-month deposits at 5 per cent** funding a **fixed 7 per cent 5-year loan**: when deposits are **renewed at 6 per cent**, NII falls from 2 to **1 per cent**; at **8 per cent**, it turns **negative**. The reverse (long fixed deposits funding short floating advances) hurts when rates **fall**.

**Repricing risk:** assets and liabilities are placed in buckets by **repricing date** (not maturity). **Gap = rate sensitive assets - rate sensitive liabilities**; shown as an **amount**, a **ratio (RSA / RSL)** or a **percentage**; monitored against **limits**.

- More **rate sensitive liabilities** than assets in a bucket: bank **gains when rates fall**, **loses when they rise**.
- More **rate sensitive assets**: the reverse.

**Tools:** swaps to change **fixed to floating** or the reverse; **VaR, present value, duration and simulation**. Capital is required for **market risk**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A bucket with more sensitive liabilities than assets is hurt by rising rates.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Rate sensitive assets minus rate sensitive liabilities in a time bucket.

payload.title: Repricing gap, sensitivity ratio and NII effect
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Gap = RSA - RSL.**

**Sensitivity ratio = RSA / RSL.**

**Change in NII = Gap x change in interest rate** (for the period).

Example: RSA **Rs 600 crore**, RSL **Rs 800 crore** in the 6-month bucket: gap **-200**; ratio **0.75**. If rates **rise 1 per cent**: change in NII = **-200 x 0.01 = -Rs 2 crore a year** (in the bucket).

variables.name: Rate sensitive assets in the bucket
Rate sensitive liabilities in the bucket

assumptions: Assets and liabilities reprice at the start of the bucket
common_errors: Using maturity instead of repricing date
Ignoring the direction of the gap

payload.expanded_explanation_md: A negative gap loses income when rates rise.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the effect on NII of a 1 per cent rise when the gap is minus Rs 200 crore?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A fall of about Rs 2 crore a year.

payload.title: The role of treasury in ALM
payload.core_explanation_md:
The balance sheet carries **large market risk**; treasury links **core banking** with **financial markets**, so market risk is **identified and monitored through treasury**.

- Mismatches **cannot be removed by moving assets or liabilities** across time bands, and **some mismatch earns profit**; treasury uses **derivatives and new products** to bridge gaps.
- Treasury trading positions create their own **market risk**, sometimes **compensating**; only the **residual risk** is hedged.
- **Credit products** are replaced by marketable treasury products (**commercial paper** instead of working capital).
- The **ALM desk** sits in the dealing room, or an **ALCO support group** in treasury; the **treasury head** is a member of **ALCO**, contributing to **pricing and policy**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Treasury is the bank window onto the market and so the natural manager of its market risk.

self_check.prompt_text: Who from treasury sits on ALCO?

payload.title: Using derivatives in ALM
payload.core_explanation_md:
Derivatives **replicate market movements** to offset the risks in ordinary products, and need **little capital** (margin only on exchange traded). They can hedge **one big deal** or **aggregate balance sheet risk** (which needs **dynamic** management).

**Examples:**

1. **3-year fixed loan funded by 3-month deposits** (cheap, but repriced 12 times): **swap** the floating deposit cost into **fixed for 3 years** (receive T-bill-linked floating, pay fixed): the **spread is protected**.
2. **Deposit at T-bill + 1 per cent, loan yields T-bill + 3 per cent**: **spread 2 per cent** protected by a swap that makes the loan return floating.
3. **USD borrowed at 3 per cent, lent in rupees at 6.5 per cent**, forward cover cost **1.5 per cent**: **spread 6.5 - 3 - 1.5 = 2 per cent**.

Currency mismatch: **call options** to repay foreign currency loans, **put options** to protect foreign currency receivables.

**Limitations:** product rates may not follow the benchmark; **embedded options** (prepayment) cannot be fully hedged; **basis risk** remains; the market and the dealers' skills must be developed.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A swap fixes the funding cost so a fixed loan spread is locked in.

self_check.prompt_text: What residual risk remains after a derivative hedge that does not match the exposure exactly?

payload.title: Credit risk, securitisation and credit derivatives
payload.core_explanation_md:
Treasury credit risk is mostly **counterparty risk within limits**, but treasury meets lending through:

- **Credit substitutes:** **commercial paper and corporate bonds**, which can be **marked to market** and **sold at a discount** if credit quality falls: more flexible than a loan.
- **Securitisation:** loan receivables turned into tradable **pass-through certificates (PTCs)** through a **special purpose vehicle (SPV)**, **freeing capital** for fresh lending.

**Credit derivatives** (credit default swap, credit linked note) **separate credit risk from the asset** and transfer it to a **protection seller** for a **fee**:

- **Protection buyer** pays a **premium (credit default spread, a percentage of notional a year)**.
- **Protection seller** pays **principal on default** of the **reference entity** (a **credit event**).

**Lessons of 2008-09:** institutions securitised assets **without careful assessment**; protection sellers had **counterparty risk**; derivatives are **highly leveraged** (tiny fee, huge notional). The central bank allowed **single name CDS on corporate bonds** with eligibility norms (not taught).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Credit risk moves to the protection seller but counterparty risk to that seller replaces it.

self_check.prompt_text: Who pays the premium in a credit default swap?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The protection buyer pays the credit default spread to the protection seller.

payload.title: Credit default swap premium
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Annual premium = CDS spread x notional.**

**Premium for a period = CDS spread x notional x days/365.**

**Payment on default = notional x (1 - recovery rate)** (protection seller pays the loss after recovery; courseware says the protection seller pays principal on default of the reference obligation).

Example: notional **Rs 100 crore**, spread **1.5 per cent**: premium **Rs 1.5 crore a year**.

assumptions: Spread applied to the full notional
common_errors: Charging spread on the recovery value only
Forgetting the recovery rate in the default payout

payload.expanded_explanation_md: The fee is small relative to notional, which is why the leverage is high.

self_check.prompt_text: How is the annual CDS premium computed?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The CDS spread multiplied by the notional.

payload.title: Transfer pricing
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Transfer pricing** fixes the **cost of funds and return on assets** of the bank rationally: **treasury notionally buys and sells** the bank's deposits and loans, and the price is the basis for judging **profitability of banking activity**.

**Treasury price = market interest rate + cost of hedging market risk + cost of reserve assets.**

**Example:** banking department takes a deposit at **7 per cent**; treasury buys it at **6 per cent** (market, net of hedging and liquidity); the **1 per cent difference is borne by the banking department**. It lends at **10 per cent** and sells the loan to treasury at **7 per cent**: the **3 per cent balance** is the **risk premium** earned by the banking side.

Once in place, **treasury carries the liquidity and interest rate risk** of the whole bank and credit departments show **only credit risk**. It helps measure **branch profitability**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Prices differ by tenor and maturity.

self_check.prompt_text: Who bears the market risk of mismatches once transfer pricing is applied?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Treasury, so credit departments reflect only credit risk.

payload.title: Spread under transfer pricing
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Banking department spread on a loan = loan rate - transfer price of funds.**

**Banking department cost of a deposit = deposit rate - treasury price for the deposit** (a charge when positive).

**Treasury spread = transfer price of the loan - transfer price of the deposit** for matched amounts.

Example: loan at **10**, transfer price **7**: **3 per cent** to the lending branch; deposit at **7**, treasury price **6**: branch **loses 1 per cent**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Branch profit depends on the transfer price assigned, so the policy must be fair.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the branch spread on a 10 per cent loan funded at a transfer price of 7 per cent?

payload.title: The integrated risk management policy
payload.core_explanation_md:
ALM needs a **strong policy foundation**. The **integrated risk management policy** includes:

| Policy | Content |
| --- | --- |
| **ALM policy** | **ALCO** composition, risk measures, monitoring, pricing, MIS, protecting **NIM** |
| **Liquidity policy** | **Minimum liquidity**, **reserve funding**, **money market limits**, **contingent funding**, committed lines |
| **Derivatives policy** | **Norms for use**, **capital allocation**, restrictions, valuation, exposure limits |
| **Investment policy** | Permissible investments, **rating and listing norms**, **SLR and non-SLR**, private placements, classification, valuation, repos |
| **Composite policy for forex and treasury** | Merchant and trading positions, **exposure, intra-day and overnight limits, stop-loss, valuation** |
| **Transfer pricing policy** | **Methodology**, **spreads retained by treasury**, allocation of costs |

Also a **money laundering prevention policy** and a **hedging policy** for customer risks. **Credit and operational risk policies** are outside ALCO.

**Requirements:** approved at the **highest level (Board or committee)**, **compliant** with regulations and market codes (**FIMMDA, FEDAI**), **monitored** by senior executives, **reviewed annually** and often **filed** with the central bank.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Policies set the limits within which dealers and ALCO operate.

self_check.prompt_text: At what level must the risk policies be approved?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The highest level: the Board or a Board committee.

payload.stem_md: In the 6-month bucket a bank has rate sensitive assets of Rs 600 crore and rate sensitive liabilities of Rs 800 crore. What is the repricing gap (Rs crore, as a shortfall)?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the size of the negative gap as a positive number.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Gap = 600 - 800 = -200, a shortfall of Rs 200 crore.

payload.stem_md: For the same bucket, what is the sensitivity ratio (to 2 decimal places)?
Interest rates rise by 1 per cent. By how much does annual net interest income fall because of the Rs 200 crore negative gap (Rs crore)?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the size of the fall as a positive number.

payload.stem_md: Deposits of Rs 100 crore costing 5 per cent fund a fixed 7 per cent loan. The deposits renew at 6.5 per cent. What is the new net interest income for the year (Rs crore, to 1 decimal place)?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Interest earned 7, paid 6.5, NII = Rs 0.5 crore.

payload.stem_md: A bank borrows USD at 3.00 per cent for 6 months and lends equivalent rupees at 6.50 per cent. The forward premium cost of cover is 1.50 per cent. What is its hedged spread (per cent)?
A deposit is priced at T-bill plus 1 per cent and the loan yields T-bill plus 3 per cent. What is the spread (per cent)?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Spread = (T + 3) - (T + 1) = 2 per cent whatever the T-bill rate.

payload.stem_md: A 3-year loan is funded by 3-month deposits. How many times is the deposit repriced during the life of the loan?
A bank buys credit protection on Rs 200 crore at a credit default spread of 1.25 per cent a year. What is the annual premium (Rs crore, to 2 decimal places)?
The reference entity defaults and recovery is 40 per cent. What loss payment (Rs crore) does the protection seller make on the Rs 200 crore notional?
A branch lends at 10.50 per cent and the transfer price of funds is 7.25 per cent. What is its spread (per cent, to 2 decimal places)?
A branch raises deposits at 7.00 per cent and treasury buys them at 6.00 per cent. On Rs 300 crore, what is the annual charge borne by the branch (Rs crore)?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the size of the charge as a positive number.

payload.stem_md: In the 8-14 day bucket, cash outflows are Rs 900 crore and inflows Rs 780 crore. What is the gap (Rs crore, as a shortfall)?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the size of the shortfall as a positive number.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Gap = 780 - 900 = -120, a shortfall of Rs 120 crore.

payload.stem_md: Assume the net cumulative negative mismatch limit in a bucket is 10 per cent of cumulative outflows of Rs 3,000 crore. What is the maximum shortfall allowed (Rs crore)?
